label: H.R. 10503

selection.reason: Impact scored and summarised by Gemini. (rated before the current eligibility rules; kept)

summary: H.R. 10503 establishes a federal grant program managed by the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development to reimburse specific states for costs incurred and damages caused by widespread federal immigration enforcement activities. It transfers over $139 billion from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection funds to finance this grant program, which distributes money to eligible states, nonprofits, and small businesses.

affected_groups.effect: May apply for grants to receive reimbursement for costs and damages from specified federal immigration operations.
affected_groups.group: Eligible States (Minnesota, California, Illinois, Louisiana, Maine, North Carolina, and Oregon)

affected_groups.effect: Receive funds transferred from state grants to support impacted educational institutions, healthcare and psychosocial support, local government operations, and investigations or memorialization.
Receive funds transferred from state grants to address impacts from the operations.
Have $139,575,630,000 of their available funds under Public Law 119-21 transferred to the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development.
affected_groups.group: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection

key_provisions: Requires the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development to establish a grant program within 60 days of enactment to reimburse states for costs and damages from increased immigration enforcement activities.
Transfers $139,575,630,000 from funds made available for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection under Public Law 119-21 to fund the program.

Lists eligible states and their corresponding operations: Minnesota (Operation Metro Surge), California, Illinois (Operation Midway Blitz), Louisiana (Operation Swamp Sweep and Catahoula Crunch), Maine (Operation Catch of the Day), North Carolina (Operation Charlottes Web), and Oregon (Operation Black Rose).
Requires the Secretary to establish criteria for grants including lost economic activity, estimated local government costs, and community harm.

Mandates that recipient states transfer grant funds to tax-exempt 501(c)(3) organizations for educational support, healthcare, local government support, and commissions of inquiry, as well as to impacted small businesses.
Assigns program oversight to the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Housing and Urban Development and requires a Government Accountability Office study and report within 30 days.
Terminates the grant program three years after its establishment.
missing_information: Exact individual grant amounts each eligible state would receive
Specific details on the exact criteria or formulas the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development will use to award the grants beyond the minimum requirements
summary_detail.plain_summary: H.R. 10503 establishes a federal grant program managed by the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development to reimburse specific states for costs incurred and damages caused by widespread federal immigration enforcement activities. It transfers over $139 billion from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection funds to finance this grant program, which distributes money to eligible states, nonprofits, and small businesses.
summary_detail.significance: The bill involves the transfer of a substantial amount of federal funding—over $139 billion—from federal immigration enforcement agencies to a housing and urban development grant program aimed at reimbursing seven specific states and supporting local nonprofits and small businesses for impacts tied to federal immigration enforcement.

title: To establish a Federal grant program to reimburse certain States for the costs incurred and damage caused by widespread deployment of Federal immigration officials, and for other purposes.
